speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member has previously asked this question. In fact he asked it two weeks ago during a hearing of the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration. I pointed out to the hon. member at that time, and I suppose I should repeat what I said, that we already adjusted the figures substantially last December when we put a major restraint on skilled workers coming into Canada to the mining industry, the construction industry and in 24 categories of the manufacturing industry. That is the answer we gave to the hon. member at that time. INQUIRY WHETHER AGREEMENT WILL BE MADE BETWEEN PRATT & WHITNEY, MONTREAL, AND UNIONS

Madam Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. The minister is aware of the substantial and generous government contributions and subsidies received by Pratt & Whitney in Montreal. Despite these subsidies, the company has been obliged to lay off over 1,500 employees, and although the minister has set up a new work-sharing program and the unions seem to be very interested, there is still no agreement with the company on this matter. Since the government, in subsidizing this company, has a certain responsibility, would the minister, for the sake of all the employees involved, be prepared to send one of his officials to make a special effort to conclude an agreement between the company and the unions, and thus prevent the loss of thousands of jobs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the discussions between the management of Pratt & Whitney, the union officials and the government have been ongoing now for several weeks. The whole essence of the work-sharing program is based upon the voluntary co-operation of the three major partners. We cannot compel either management or the union to come into an agreement; it must be based upon their willingness to come into that agreement.
We have signed a work-sharing arrangement with the office workers of Pratt & Whitney. It is really up to the union and management to overcome their own jurisdictional disputes as to who is included in the voting arrangements in order for the work-sharing to apply to the general work force. We are providing a member of our manpower consultative services, a separate division of my department, to try to bring that agreement about. We will continue to work with them at any time, but it is based upon mutual co-operation between the three partners. We would ask the hon. member to use his good offices to help that agreement come about. It would be a very important support and assistance for the workers there, if they could get the work-sharing agreement signed.

April 20, 1982

been given a very broad mandate indeed. It wants to demonstrate great care and concern for those affected by the offshore drilling operations.
I would remind my hon. friend that the investigations to which he is referring are internal investigations of the existing United States agencies. It is obviously much easier and faster to set up such investigations than a joint inquiry of the type we are setting up. As I said, our inquiry has a much broader mandate. However, there is work being done, both by the companies concerned and by agencies of the Government of Canada, in gathering evidence and carrying out studies to be made available to the commission as soon as the commission requests the information.
Concerning the presence of observers before the United States agencies, I am not in a position to advise my friend as to whether there is an observer today or not. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to enter into debate on this bill, which basically is legislation designed to bring into effect the federal government's petroleum incentives program.
Members of Parliament come to this House from varied occupations and professions, and there is a strength in that diversity. As elected representatives we serve the Canadians who sent us to this House. We also have an opportunity to serve the professions and the occupations at which we once earned a living. This is one of those opportunities when I as a Member of Parliament have an opportunity to serve my former
profession in Parliament. For that reason I intend to be as nonpartisan in my remarks as possible.
I also beg the indulgence of the House to outline the background which lies behind my concerns with respect to this legislation.
Twenty-five years ago I entered upon the study of chartered accountancy as a chartered accountant student with my father's firm in Toronto, Horace G. Lewis and Company. I graduated as a chartered accountant in September, 1962. Although I have not practised regularly, I am still a member in good standing of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Ontario.
There are five hon. members in this House who are members of the accounting profession. They are the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke), the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson) and myself on this side. On the government side there is the hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Demers) and the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Desmarais). All of us are proud to be members of the accounting profession.
The Institute of Chartered Accountants of Canada was formed in 1902. It was first named the Dominion Association of Chartered Accountants. There were six provincial institutes at that time, the earliest being the Ontario and Quebec institutes of chartered accountancy formed in 1879. The Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants has been responsible for setting accounting standards since 1946.
With that background in mind I wish to address two issues with respect to this bill. The first is the generally accepted accounting principles which are applicable to the treatment of payments under the petroleum incentives program. The second is the position of the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants and the repercussions if that position is ignored.
The Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants has an active program of ongoing accounting research which is supported by members of the accounting profession from across Canada. In September 1975, the institute enacted Section 3800 of the CICA handbook to account for direct payments of all types of government assistance. That section was produced as a result of a rigorous discussion and debate of all possible alternatives by members of the CICA accounting research committee, consultation with their associates, exposure of proposed standards to the accounting profession and the business community for comment and consideration of all comments received before the standard was formally issued. Because of concerns as to the proper accounting treatment of the PIP grants, formally known as the Petroleum Incentives Program incentives, the CICA initiated discussions in early 1981 with the oil industry, individual companies, their auditors, and representatives of the federal government.
April 20, 1982

In April, 1981 the accounting research steering committee drafted a proposed accounting guideline for the treatment of PIP incentive grants. The accounting research committee discussed the draft guideline and expressed agreement with the steering committee's position and proposed course of action. The draft guideline was then circulated to interested parties for comment. Government representatives, including the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), received the draft guideline but did not offer any comments on it.
In January 1982 a final draft of the guideline was circulated by the accounting research committee to the petroleum industry, through the Canadian Petroleum Association and the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada, and to other interested parties for comment. None of the recipients expressed objections to the final guidelines. At the same time, government representatives, including the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), were advised of the steering committee's intention to finalize and issue the guideline.
The CICA then issued a formal accounting guideline dated February, 1982 which specified that PIP incentives should be accounted for in accordance with the CICA handbook, Section 3800. Basically, that section specifies that since petroleum incentives are expenditure oriented, they should be taken into income in the same manner as the exploration and development expenditures they support.
Some oil companies have made representations to the federal government as to the acceptability of a different type of accounting treatment. Discussions have taken place between representatives of the oil industry and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources which present the possibility of federal action to legitimize an accounting treatment which is contrary to the CICA position and thus contrary to generally accepted accounting principles. The dangers inherent in such actions prompt my remarks today.
One of the most basic of the generally accepted accounting principles is that revenues and expenditures related to those revenues should be matched as closely as possible. The February 1982 accounting guideline issued by the CICA defines the PIP grants as follows:
The petroleum incentives program provides for direct incentive payments for exploration and development to Canadian taxable and non-taxable corporations and individuals. The objective is to encourage oil and gas exploration by Canadian corporations and individuals.
Therefore, the petroleum incentives should be taken into income in the same manner as the exploration and development expenditures they support. On the other hand, the petroleum and gas revenue tax is a tax payable by corporations and individuals, including federal and provincial enterprises, that receive income from oil and gas production. It is levied on net operating revenue related to the production of oil and gas, including income from oil and gas royalty interests.
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
The controversy arises because corporations and individuals qualifying for the PIP grants may waive entitlement to the direct payment of the grant and instead receive the benefits by way of a credit against the petroleum and gas revenue tax. It is then suggested that since the PGRT is a current expense, the PIP grant should be included in current earnings by netting or offsetting the PIP grants against the PGRT in the income statement.
The remarks of my good friend, Gert Mulcahy, F.C.A., CICA accounting research director, are most pertinent and succinct. She said:
The proper accounting for government grants, including PIP grants, is largely a question of timing. PIP grants should be taken into income as the exploration and development efforts they finance result in earnings or the expenditures are written off . .. If such grants were to be taken into income immediately, the result would be current overstated earnings for affected Canadian companies and reduced earnings for those companies in the future ... Economic reality is not reflected if a grant for future benefit is included in income for the current year before the results of the exploration expenditures are known.
There is some suggestion that the oil companies are pressuring the minister to allow the "offset" or "netting" treatment. In my opinion, that is not a generally accepted accounting treatment and I would urge the federal government to support the CICA position rather than enacting an order in council legislating generally accounting principles. We can understand the oil companies's concern to present as favourable an income position as possible but I suggest to the government that this can be accomplished through the statement of changes in financial position included in the companies's financial statements.
As suggested in the accounting handbook, the method by which benefits are received should not affect the accounting treatment. It is also suggested by the oil companies that since the PIP grants were instituted by the federal government because of the elimination of the earned depletion allowances and the super-depletion allowances for frontier exploration, the grants should be allowed as deductions from income.
With respect, Mr. Speaker, that argument does not necessarily apply. No government can eliminate apples and replace them with oranges and then legislate the oranges into apples. That is what the government is trying to do.
That concludes my remarks as to the generally accepted accounting principles and the CICA efforts in this case. I now wish to turn my attention to the position of the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants and the possible repercussions of actions contrary to that position.
The Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants and the related provincial institutes take a back seat to no professional body when it comes to professional research, professional independence and professional responsibility. My previous remarks make it unnecessary for me to elaborate upon the ongoing concerns of the CICA with respect to the need for professional research of a high calibre. This is a perfect example of the methods by which the CICA operates and it would be difficult for any profession to find fault with those methods. If the federal government is putting forth a contrary position, it should prove its point through the force of research

April 20, 1982
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
and logic and through discussion with the accounting profession.
As professionals, chartered accountants guard their independence jealously. Accounts have been lost because chartered accountants refused to bend to the client's interests. Confidence in that independence is reflected in the reported remarks of Henry Knowles, Chairman of the Ontario Securities Commission. He suggests the accounting profession is "a major defender of investor rights" and that if the federal government legislates generally accepted accounting principles "it will destroy the credibility of the accounting profession as a self-regulating and policing organization".
Professions earn respect by being responsible. The easy way out for the CICA would have been to bow to the federal government's wishes and adopt their ideas or accept an order in council legalizing the treatment of PIP grants as an offset to the PGRT. To the CICA's credit, they have not capitulated, but under the leadership of their president, Dennis F. Culver, FCA, they have continued to press their arguments through consultation.
We have recently had an excellent example of the dangers which arise, Mr. Speaker, when government fails to consult industry, labour, or related professions and occupations. The November budget is a perfect example of what can happen when bureaucrats try to legislate tax reform without consultation. The result is chaos. The CICA accounting research guideline is an excellent example of what can happen when a profession takes the initiative and demonstrates professional responsibility. The result is an independent standard which governments, investors, the profession and the industry can look to for guidance. If the federal government legislates a treatment of PIP grants in financial statements which contravenes CICA guidelines, then there are some very real problems ahead. Auditors may be forced to comment upon the treatment in their report, as to whether or not it is in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, as they are known throughout the world. Securities commissions in Canada and foreign countries may require the CICA treatment, thus leading to investor confusion. The self-governing integrity of the CICA would be damaged.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the state may legislate the relevant professional committees of a hospital to ensure a high level of medical competence, but the state does not tell a doctor how to remove an appendix; the profession determines that. The state may legislate legal aid for every accused to ensure a legal defence, but the state does not tell a lawyer how to examine a witness. That is a matter for the profession.
By the same token the federal government may, through this bill, legislate PIP grants; but it is the accounting profession through its committees which should determine how those grants are treated in financial statements.
I close, Mr. Speaker, by urging the minister to adopt the CICA position on this issue because it is in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and as an indication
of the respect of the federal government for the efforts of CICA to maintain generally accepted accounting principles and its professional independence.

The energy critic of the Conservative party, the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), wrote to the minister on December 21, 1981. In his letter he said that "the parts of the proposed bill dealing with the Canadian ownership rate and petroleum incentives program are long overdue and we would be willing to see two relevant acts introduced and dealt with on a priority basis".
I wonder if the hon. member would indicate why his party, having asked that they be brought forward on a priority basis and having said that they are long overdue, is now opposing the Canadian ownership rate and the petroleum incentives program?
Tell the hon. member to read my speech.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I tried to approach this subject as a Member of Parliament with some background in the accounting profession. My remarks were specifically directed to accounting treatment. I also commented that I would try to be non-partisan in my remarks. I think you will have noticed, sir, that there were no references to political positions being taken in my remarks.
The remarks of my colleague, the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), were directed to the bills themselves, and I am perfectly willing to go along with his advice on that. However, what I tried to bring to the House was an understanding of accounting treatment, and an understanding of the importance of having an independent accounting profession. My remarks were simply based on that very important principle.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have you in the chair today. I would like to direct some of my remarks to the hon. member's question as to why we oppose the bill in principle at this time. The hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) just spoke with eloquence as to the need for proper accounting procedures. I think we will find many oil companies in Canada will need to acquire many more accountants in order to deal with the petroleum incentives program and the Canadian ownership rate, and the difficulties which will result in the next couple of months as they try to sort out this bill as it passes through Parliament.
At the same time we have seen the tremendous impact the NEP has had on our oil and gas industry. The PIP grants were needed a year or a year and a half ago. They will now do relatively little to assist the industry to get back to the position it was in some while ago. Part of the problem is that by far the
April 20, 1982

majority of people in Canada do not understand the operations of the oil and gas industry. That is a problem which not only Members of Parliament and those people involved in the industry for 40 or more years have to face, but it is also a problem for the industry and its employees. They have over the years done relatively little in the way of educating the public at large as to how their operations work. Then when we are faced with the NEP, faced with a government which has used this industry as a whipping boy for everything that they find people mistrust about capitalism, it is very difficult to put their views forward as to the proper operation of their industry, what alternatives there were to the public Canadianization of the industry, and the kinds of incentives and taxation procedures necessary to take away some of the excess profits of the industry as world prices went up, and yet at the same time not destroy the industry.
The drilling industry, for example, was faced not only with the NEP, but at the same time it was hit with high interest rates. They were drilling at a very high rate and finding lots of natural gas, if not so much oil. They were then faced with an oversupply of natural gas with the resulting low cash flow because they could not market the gas. Then there were the uncertainties involved in a lack of agreement between the federal and provincial governments on taxation. In addition, there was the problem that it has taken over a year to define the National Energy Program by way of legislation. We now find a reluctance on the part of investors, domestic and foreign, to invest in the drilling industry and so we are faced with some very serious difficulties in obtaining the funds to get the drilling industry going again.
Now, in addition to that tremendous lack of knowledge which I spoke of about how the industry works, we have here in Ottawa a group of public servants and deputy ministers along with the minister who, I feel, at that time knew very little about how the industry evolved and how it had been so successful in finding oil and gas. In fact, through natural processes much of the industry was being bought and taken over by small Canadian firms.
That is the way we should have proceeded with a national energy program. But here we had a minister supported and pushed by his public servants to bring in his National Energy Program which has hurt the nation so badly. Think of what has happened to the goal of energy self-sufficiency. Think of the number of jobs lost, rigs lost, the severe damage to small companies, and the increasing number of small Canadian companies declaring bankruptcy. When the program was put in place it affected many more people in this country than the minister or his public servants who supported him could ever imagine. They had no idea of the effect their program would have on this country. Perhaps they were prepared to take the risks because of a feeling that Alberta was doing too well or that the western provinces were doing too well as far as oil and gas revenues were concerned. Maybe it was thought that with drilling taking place offshore on the east coast as well as the Beaufort Sea, some capital should be moved into those areas
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
and by doing that we would have some success and it would all be worth it.
However, that has not come about. The people who have been involved in the industry and the provinces so affected by the oil and gas industry cannot trust this government to put forward an objective picture of the oil and gas industry. Many companies, provinces and Members of Parliament have recognized this. Television and newspaper ads are now being placed by the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada, the Canadian Petroleum Association, and other independent companies to show how industry works. These ads show the types of employment the industry creates and the opportunities available to young Canadians for work. There are opportunities to take over parts of companies to a large extent now foreign owned so as to achieve greater Canadian ownership. These kinds of ads and education procedures are continuing. At the same time people are being told about the devastation which has taken place in the industry.
Those of us who represent areas which produce oil and gas are receiving hundreds more calls from people who are being laid off. We are receiving calls from companies that just a year ago were looking at a bright future but are now bankrupt. We realize that we have to do a lot more to educate our colleagues about how this industry works. We have to get across what kinds of alternatives there are in order to see the vision that we wish as far as Canadian ownership is concerned. At the same time we must not create the dilemmas now being faced in the oil and gas industry.
There are alternatives to this bill which introduces the Canadian ownership rate. Some alternatives were put forward in the 1979 budget that was defeated. In it an offer was made to Canadian citizens to invest in oil and gas companies. In return some capital gains relief would be given. There was also a provision for directing the incentives program to the small Canadian-owned oil and gas companies are respecting the taxation procedures to be used as far as profits of the large companies were concerned. Those were the alternatives that were available, but instead the oil industry was used as a whipping boy by this government. It was used to foster Canadian nationalism in the sense of nationalization of companies run by Canadian governments and Crown corporations.
In reply to a question yesterday, the minister in defence of the National Energy Program said that in the last year we have gained 6 per cent more Canadian ownership. That is probably true. If one looks at the acquisitions of Petro-Canada and Dome Petroleum, some large companies were bought out. But what was the cost of doing that? Canadian taxpayers have put over $1.5 billion into Petro-Canada. Petro-Canada itself has borrowed in the billions of dollars in the private sector to buy out some foreign-owned oil companies. They have not found much more oil. All that has been accomplished is the purchase of more oil already discovered.
Another cost of the National Energy Prgram was lost jobs, about which I will go into detail in a few minutes. Also as a

Petroleum Incentives Program Act
result of this program we have seen the loss of service companies and drilling rigs. The program has also caused the bankruptcies of companies. This program has contributed to the high interest rates that we are facing now as much money flows out of Canada. It was necessary to attract American dollars into Canada in order that we could pay our debts to other countries, and for purchasing offshore oil which had to be paid for in American dollars. Our interest rates had to be raised to attract money back into Canada. We have caused severe damage to the small Canadian-owned oil and gas companies and to the people who serviced those companies in many communities across the nation. Those are the costs of this National Energy Program.
Mr. Don Pack, President of the Canadian Association of Oilwell Drilling Contractors, which association comprises small Canadian-owned companies, has said:
The replacement value of the rigs that have left Canada in the past year exceeds $1 billion. You might equate this loss and the impact on a community, to the loss of one hundred $10 million manufacturing plants, each directly employing 52 people. The difference in operating levels this year and last in the drilling industry alone has resulted in a direct loss of employment for over 8,000 skilled rig crew members.
For 1982, we see a further erosion of the Canadian drilling and service fleet with increasing loss in employment. During 1982 approximately 6,000 wells will be drilled in western Canada, a decline of 33 per cent from the peak established in 1980 and by mid-summer less than 200 rigs will be active. For a country importing approximately 200,000 barrels a day of crude oil from foreign producers at a cost of $8,000,000 per day, this is a tragedy.
I think that figure of 200,000 barrels a day of crude oil is rather low. The figure is more like 400,000 or 450,000 barrels a day. Mr. Pack continues:
The energy balance in the world is finely tuned and vulnerable to disruption and price shock. Disruption in Canada's supply of oil, before we are selfsufficient, is a sure bet.
The following statistics are as a result of the National Energy Program. Drilling activity in Canada is down 25 per cent in 1981 compared to 1980. In the United States in the same period drilling activity was up 26 per cent. A record 78,884 wells were drilled in the United States. That figure increased by 16,000 from the previous year. On the other hand, Canada's figures were down substantially. Our well completions totalled 7,183, down from 9,481 in 1980. Development drilling was down 28 per cent to 4,000 from 5,556 in 1980. Total metres drilled confirmed this decline. The number dropped from 10.27 million metres in 1980 to 7.64 million metres in 1981. This is a decline of 26 per cent.
Since the announcement of the National Energy Program in 1980, 226 drilling rigs have left Canada. At the end of 1981 only 52 per cent of Canada's total of 443 drilling rigs were active and the activities of many seismic crews were down 25 per cent. Many of these people were active in my constituency and in the constituencies of my neighbouring Members of Parliament in Alberta and Saskatchewan.
There are many examples of Canadian entrepreneurs who are suffering the consequences. For example, there is Raydan Transport in Nisku. Statistics do not mean a lot to many people until they are translated into human terms. I have seen the human casualties of the National Energy Program in my
riding. Many companies in a once thriving and prosperous area are starting to sell and move rigs to the United States. Many of them are throwing up their hands and giving up, which is helping the Western Canada Concept party.
I should like to cite an example of something which happened approximately two weeks ago. It shows the effects of the National Energy Program on a trucking company which was once prosperous. Raydan Transport of Nisku was a major rig moving company. It began liquidating $8 million worth of equipment assets. It received a little over $2.6 million for those assets, if I have read the bill of sale correctly. Bill English, the president of the company, said that this action was taken as a result of taking a good look at what was happening to the trucking industry. Until last month Raydan operated 75 trucks and back-up equipment and employed over 100 people. Now it expects to need only five employees and will only operate two to five trucks in 1982.
Why has the company lost over $1 million in the last 18 months? Its problems started with the NEP. Before that Raydan would move anywhere from 150 to 200 rigs per year. This dropped to only 35 rigs in 1981. It obviously had the equipment but the work was not there. On top of that situation, there was an increase in the cost of fuel, skyrocketing costs of equipment and labour, maintenance costs and high interest rates. These factors made the prospect of carrying on until there was light at the end of the tunnel very unattractive. In this instance we are looking at a company which is folding. Approximately 95 people will be out of work as a result of misguided government policy. This is happening all over my riding. The Nisku Industrial Park which was based on oil and gas activities has lost many people and firms in the last year.
What are some people saying in regard to the entire situation? One answer came from the provincial government which brought in a royalty reduction plan. It is intending to rollback royalties. It is an answer to many people involved in the industry. Now they can come to the provincial government and say that they desperately need some assistance until changes are made in the federal government. The provincial government brought in a rollback in royalties which will have an effect upon the industry. Most of the money acquired by the rollback in royalties will be needed to pay off debts which have accumulated in the last 1.5 years. We may not see the activity which is necessary to bring back the oil and gas industry of Alberta.
This morning I spoke with some small businessmen in my riding who are involved in the industry. They said that there has been a great improvement in attitude because of the movement of the Alberta government in rolling back royalties, but they warned that it was not enough. If complementary action is not taken quickly by the federal government as far as the taxes in the National Energy Program are concerned, conditions will revert to where they were beforehand.
As I said, in the last year some huge debts were built up by many of these companies. Many small Canadian companies are involved in the drilling and servicing of the oil industry and do not have much royalty income. As a result, these companies

which are facing bankruptcies and laying off employees will not obtain much benefit from the rollback of royalties. Additional incentives to the oil industry are needed. I suppose some will be included in the petroleum incentives program, but much more will be needed, especially as world oil prices and consumption drop. Also we must remember that there is the huge shut-in of oil and gas in Alberta and Saskatchewan at the present time. There is a need to help some companies as far as taxes are concerned if we are to remove some of the suffering from the oil industry. They are truly Canadian companies. They are local, they are Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia operations, yet they are being stifled by federal policies which claim to promote Canadian ownership. This points out the grave contradiction between the philosophy of the National Energy Program and its actual effect. The government must look very seriously at making some changes to get these small operations back on their feet and producing again.
According to Wilfred Gobert of Peters and Co. Ltd. of
Calgary:
The retroactive provincial royalty tax credit, imminent Alberta petroleum incentive payments and gas take-or-pay proposals by TransCanada PipeLines Ltd. of Calgary will all mean additional money for the industry this year.
But like other analysts, he expects that the industry will use the additional funds to pay off debts first before rushing into more exploration and development spending. Mr. Gobert went
on to say:
The Alberta royalty changes could mark an end to the slump in exploration and development this year. We may have hit bottom ...
The worst of the exploration and development activity could be behind us.
It will need an extra push, and that push can only come from the national government in the form of some reduction in high taxes.
We are feeling the downturn in that industry. We are starting to feel it more than ever 1.5 years after the National Energy Program. The cash flows of larger companies are down between 25 to 40 per cent. There is some belt-tightening which is being felt not only by workers but by many executives. Gulf, Turbo Resources and Dome Petroleum have laid off over 1,150 people in the last week. Even Petro-Canada has felt the pinch and is finding that it must release some of its employees. They are all facing as well a tremendous paper burden which results from the bills before the House and the extra accounting procedures being put in place because of federal and provincial programs.
It was interesting to read the words of United States Congressman John D. Dingell who said that this year more than 12 per cent of the oil and gas exploration in the United States will be conducted by Canadian companies, many of which are from my area, using workers and equipment that have shifted drilling to the United States. If past experience is any indication, they will not return to Canada until the government alters its course. In short, the government's policies are having the exact opposite effect to their stated purpose. Those policies have already shown themselves to be actually injuring the Canadian economy, driving venture capital from the nation
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
and impairing the strength of the Canadian dollar. That American congressman is seeing the same effects of the National Energy Program as we are seeing on this side of the House. They are reaping the benefits of our expertise and our drilling.
Although we may not have had ownership of the oil industry when the National Energy Program was introduced, we did have control and many of us wonder why we did not use that control to determine the kind of taxation policies we could have put forward so as to use the abundant moneys which flowed from that industry to provide incentives to the small oil companies and start the megaprojects operating in Canada, which would have provided employment and spinoff benefits for thousands of Canadian companies and Canadian workers, instead of taking the gamble which the minister was obviously prepared to take when he introduced the National Energy Program. That gamble, which was to divert money from the prairie provinces, Alberta and British Columbia to provide the needed incentives for projects in the north, on Canada lands and on the east coast, should not have killed the industry which was providing the work and the oil and gas for Canada at the same time. That gamble may not have paid off in terms of oil self-sufficiency by 1990.
The Ocean Ranger, which tragically sank off the east coast, has put back the drilling program in that area for some time. The optimism that many of us felt regarding the Beaufort Sea did not materialize during this year's testing. Instead of a well which was estimated to produce some 30,000 barrels a day, it only produced 3,000 barrels a day. It is still our belief that there are substantial supplies of oil and gas in those areas which we should pursue with all effort, but at the same time we cannot kill an industtry which has been so successful for so many years in this country.
We need a response to the difficulties these companies are facing. In Alberta we presently have shut-in oil amounting to approximately 220,000 barrels of crude oil per day. Why is that oil shut in at the present time? Our federal government has done such an excellent job of negotiating offshore contracts that we are importing Mexican and other foreign crude oil at a rate which forces us to shut down our wells in our own country. This causes a deterioration in the amount of cash flow for those companies and causes further difficulty to that industry even beyond the National Energy Program.
I do not know how I can emphasize any more the effects of the devastation visited on our oil and gas industry by this National Energy Program and the actions of this government. If we look at the unemployment statistics in Alberta, a province that has always had the lowest unemployment in Canada, we discover that after running at less than 4 per cent throughout the 1970s and at 3.5 per cent in 1981, today we are looking at an unemployment rate of 6.7 per cent in that province. That is one of the devastating effects of this program.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to speak to this particular piece of legislation. I would like to begin by saying that we in Canada live in very serious and troubled times. A good portion of the difficulty we are experiencing is a direct result of the National Energy Program.
I think that the most disappointing news we Canadians received today was when we read in The Globe and Mail that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) will not retire at the present time while there still is an ailing economy. Most of us found that to be very disappointing news. Many of us thought that would have been one election promise that he would have upheld. But if he fails to fulfil that promise, then I cannot think of one single election promise which he made during the 1980 election campaign which has been upheld. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that this remark in the newspaper will add further to the strains on confederation and the difficulties in our economy, to the alienation and division which he has already created in this land.
I cannot think of a more hypocritical statement than that the Prime Minister cannot leave because of an ailing economy. In my view-a view which I am sure is shared by others as well-the Prime Minister has clearly wasted his mandate in dealing with the economy. He has chosen instead to address more mundane issues and has been more prone to pick fights and argue with the provinces and industry, to divide and create chaos rather than deal with the real bread and butter issues in Canada. Those issues concern jobs, interest rates, housing, energy self-sufficiency and creating a healthy and stable economic environment. He has failed to address the real problems which has affected this nation.
According to the review which was cited by various members on my side of the House which reminded the country of the conditions which existed when the Prime Minister took office, unemployment was 4.5 per cent. Today, unemployment is over 9 per cent, an additional 750,000 people unemployed. When he took office inflation was 4 per cent; today it is 11.6 per cent to 12 per cent. The current account deficit was almost in balance when he took over while today it is close to $7 billion. Bank interest rates were IVi per cent. Today, they are 15.34 per cent. At the time he took office the conventional mortgage rate was 9.2 per cent. It is I8V2 per cent today. An average house cost $21,000 in 1968 and the price today is $78,000. With respect to the post office, we could send a letter for 6 cents; today it costs 30 cents. The growth of the government has risen from 360,000 person-years to 500,000 person-years. The gross national debt was $32 billion in 1968; today it is $135 billion. The value of the dollar was 93 cents U.S. in 1968 and it is 82 cents today. It is a very dismal record and the fact that the Prime Minister will continue in office will clearly downgrade confidence in Canada and create even more anxiety and sense of hopelessness and despair.
The fact is that we live in the most difficult times we have experienced in 35 years. These hardships do not only relate to interest rates. The price of fuel would also be an interesting
comparison. We know that fuel prices have doubled in the last two years despite all those grandiose promises that fuel prices would be kept down.
But what concerns Canadians the most is that there is a feeling of hopelessness and despair in the country. Dreams are being shattered. People who have invested a lifetime of work in their farms and businesses are having their dreams shattered. Their investment of years of hard work, commitment and dedication is going out the window. There is also a fear that the worst is yet to come. The greatest improvement in confidence would be if the Prime Minister would quietly leave the scene. That action would create the greatest upturn in terms of individual confidence, economic confidence and, I am sure, in terms of international confidence.
Coupled with this economic condition which exists in Canada, we all know that there is a very deep-seated division in Canada. It is unfortunate that during the course of the last ten days when we were to have been celebrating the patriation of our Constitution, and while there was a massive celebration on Parliament Hill, there was bitterness felt throughout the country. There is not the unanimous rejoicing there should be. There is not that spirit of enthusiasm and euphoria that we experienced in 1967 during the year of our centennial celebrations. The fact is that there is deep division in this country. There is bitterness.
Much of this has been the product of this government. For example, in western Canada there is a feeling that this government governs one half of the country while it attacks the other half. That is why a separatist movement is making great inroads in western Canada. There is a separatist movement in Quebec. The statement of the Prime Minister to the effect that co-operative federalism is dead is not helping matters either, because it is part and parcel of his style of unilateralism.
I started out by saying that we are in difficult economic times and that one of the problems is directly related to the National Energy Program. There are some other reasons, and I would simply like to cite them as background to the debate on this bill. As I said earlier, the Prime Minister and his government have not really addressed the very important and fundamental issues facing this country; rather, during the last two years the government has dealt with the Constitution and other matters. There has been heavy emphasis on bilingualism, on metric, on gun control, on North-South dialogue, on building emergency civilian internment camps and things of that nature. In the meantime, the economy has been floundering.
There has also been a policy of confrontation. We know the attitude of the Prime Minister with respect to his unilateralist approach to patriation of the Constitution. We know of his approach with regard to the oil pricing agreement with the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia and of the threat that he would impose the overriding authority of
April 20, 1982

peace, order and good government to force an energy pricing agreement on the provinces whether they liked it or not. We know that the National Energy Program has been a product, not of consultation and co-operation but, rather, of unilateralism. We witnessed the decision with regard to VIA Rail. With a stroke of the pen, 20 per cent of VIA Rail passenger services were dismantled. We witnessed the actions with regard to the changes to or the emasculation of the Crowsnest Pass freight rates. While there has been some discussion, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) has suggested-
What was your position?

Well, we have some life over there! We hear the New Democratic Party is now trying to bail out, before the election, the Premier of Saskatchewan who, before the election campaign was very eager to get on with the debate on the changes to the Crowsnest Pass freight rates. That is clearly on the record. A little document was published out in Saskatchewan entitled "Eating Crow". It cites all the very positive statements of Premier Blakeney concerning the Crow and his support for the Minister of Transport's proposals to change the Crow. It is no wonder that the NDP is losing ground and support in western Canada because of the hypocrisy of the positions it takes. It takes one position here and another position out there.
Oh, oh!

I will not be sidetracked. They will be licking their wounds on Tuesday.
The fact is that the Minister of Transport said: "If there is no consensus and if you cannot agree to do it my way, we will do it that way anyway." That is the kind of unilateralism which has not augured well. It does not provide the kind of harmony and good spirit that is traditional and necessary in order for this nation to function.
The third reason we are experiencing these difficulties is the fact that we have a national economic policy based upon the redistribution of wealth rather than upon the production or generation of new wealth. Essentially, we have experienced zero growth over the last five years. There have been no incentives for the private sector or the producing sector to get on with the job of increasing the size of the national pie. If we continue along in that direction, we will not be able to provide indefinitely the kind of support and resources necessary to ensure medical care, old age pensions and assistance to the disabled. We will not be able to provide those kinds of services which would allow Canadians, who are less fortunate than those able to produce, to live a dignified lifestyle. The fact is that we have suffered zero growth and we cannot continue to support those programs under an economy functioning at that level. The only growth we have seen over the last few years has been the growth in the labour force in government. Quite frankly, about one quarter of the total labour force today is employed by some level of government. This is evident, as 42 per cent, 43 per cent or maybe even 44 per cent of the gross
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
national product is now being handled by some level of government. Of course, we cannot indefinitely continue along that path without facing some very serious difficulties.
The fourth reason we are in this period of economic stagnation and difficulty is that government policy has developed along the lines of an economy which is becoming more centrally controlled and dominated. It is a policy which is reflected and endorsed, moreover, by the recent economic development policy outlined in the budget papers. It is quite obvious that, rather than opting for tax incentives and the kind of fiscal regime which would encourage production and growth, a situation has been created in which all the resources and revenue will be recycled through government. The government will decide who the winners and who the losers will be. The government will provide the subsidies and grants and it will pick the winners and the losers. It will establish who will get a grant and where that grant shall be located, whether it will be A, B, C or D, and whether it will be located in region X, Y or Z. However, the government will decide who the winners and losers will be. If we continue to do that, I suggest we will stymie the creativity, productivity and innovation which is so necessary to maintain the growth and generation of wealth we need in this country. Furthermore, I suggest it will certainly stymie our ability to maintain the economic freedom that we want in this country. If we do not have economic freedom, there is no way we can have political freedom.
In my humble estimation, a functioning democracy cannot exist in a controlled economy. We note, with interest, the difficulty that the New Democratic Party is encountering in the province of Saskatchewan. It talks about its family of Crown corporations, some 23 Crown corporations. It refers to it as a big family. I believe the people of Saskatchewan will soundly reject that philosophy. Freedom is the issue-political and economic freedom.
We have a problem in this country which the people of the province of Saskatchewan have witnessed. The people of Saskatchewan have recognized that they can no longer tolerate the years of socialism, the years of government encroachment and the years of government interference which have stymied their economic freedom. That is the real issue in the Saskatchewan election. The people of Saskatchewan own the land. They do not want to be tenants in their own province. The government of Saskatchewan owns some two million acres of farmland.
Oh, oh!

speechtext: Oh, I cannot agree with that!

The National Energy Program is part and parcel of the issue of which I speak, the continuing government encroachment, the centrally dominated philosophy that government can make the best decision, or a government organization, structure or board can make the best decision.
I want to say this very bluntly because I have witnessed the effects of the National Energy Program. My colleague from Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) talked at great length. He lives in an area that has been both directly and indirectly affected negatively by the effects of the National Energy Program. The small industries, the small entrepreneurs, have been hurt by this program. The National Energy Program will go down in history as the man-made disaster of the eighties; there can be no question about it.
The NDP support this program. They support the principal aims and objectives of it notwithstanding the fact it has destroyed the oil industry in Saskatchewan. They are so silly, stupid and doctrinaire in terms of attitude, they have not looked at the effect of the National Energy Program on the small entrepreneur, small industry, the welder or the fabricator, and they support it.
What freedom is there for those who are employed by these small companies and have lost their jobs? The program has destroyed that industry. It has not hurt the multinationals. It is hurting the small Canadian firms, the truckers, welders, cat operators, construction workers, service workers, rig hands, drillers, those who build the fences and rights-of-way. They are the ones who are affected. They are all Canadians who work for Canadian companies.
As my colleague said, this program is working in reverse. It is destroying the viable Canadian entreprise that has been associated with the oil industry and has been so successful. Exploration was down 25 per cent to 30 per cent in 1981. It will be down another 10 or 15 per cent in 1982. All of this is in the name of Canadianization. It is not working. It is doing directly the opposite. This is really nationalization.
I listened to a couple of NDP members who spoke last night. They are not concerned about Canadianization. Their bottom line is nationalization. That is what they want. If it walks, breathes or moves, they nationalize it. If it produces, by gosh, they nationalize it double! It just does not make sense.
At the same time, the results of this policy are forcing Canadians to pay for imported oil at the rate of 500,000 barrels a day while there are locked-in supplies in Saskatchewan and Alberta. It is estimated that by the end of April, some
300,000	barrels a day of surplus oil will be locked in, not being produced in Alberta. In Saskatchewan, some 50,000 barrels a day are locked in.
The wells are shut down. People are laid off. We are bringing in oil from OPEC countries, Venezuela and Mexico at $40 a barrel. The taxpayers are subsidizing at the rate of $17.32 a barrel while $23.50 a barrel oil is left in the ground. Our work people are being dislocated. They are out of jobs. Businesses are being closed. Foreclosures and bankruptcies are occurring.
We wonder why there is alienation in western Canada. The NDP will have to answer for it. They are part and parcel of the National Energy Program. They put this government in office and are continuing to keep it there. Let them answer the people of Saskatchewan and the rest of western Canada. There are massive lay-offs in the industry. It is not hurting the multinationals. I will tell you what it is doing, Mr. Speaker. It is further eroding our balance of payments, weakening the dollar, raising our interest rates, undermining investor confidence, creating further bitterness in this land and further division. I quote from an article in the Edmonton Journal:
It has become a conventional wisdom in Canada's capital that private industry is essentially in the ripoff business and cannot be trusted. Only when industries fail and actually lay off thousands of workers do they gain credibility in Ottawa. If industries succeed, they attract suspicion among academic mandarins who see them as ripe for tax-picking.
I could include my socialist friends to my left in that category-
And they attract the political sharks who smell money where it is politically cheap to get.
That outlines the current philosophy of this government. It certainly is the philosophy that is shared by those birds over there who have never had to go out and meet a payroll or produce anything. They have been basically living as parasites off the fat of the land.
What has the National Energy Program done to a constituency like mine? In two weeks in the community of Vermilion, a small fabricating firm, Bird Oil Limited, laid off 20 people. They were in the business of fabricating storage tanks for oil. Because of the shutdown of the wells, these 20 people were laid off.
In November, 1981 in Wainwright, Alberta a small firm called Jurassic, according to an article in the Star Chronicle of November 25, was quitting Canada. I quote from the article:
"It was the hardest thing I've ever had to do."
So says Jim Voll, who laid off 30 employees here and will take Wainwright-based Jerassic Well Servicing's remaining rigs south to Oklahoma.
The decision was taken in the light of federal and provincial policies which continue to destroy the small operator, he said .. .
Government-induced depression in the oil industry here has meant there's just too little work here to remain in business, he says.
The Wainwright-based company had operated ten rigs from here, but sent six to the Oklahoma oilfields last spring. The final four will follow by the new year, Voll says, and the Wainwright office closed for good.
That is what is happening. In February, four Lloydminster firms went into receivership, displacing some 150 jobs. Petroserv Management, which also owns and operates Weldex Machine Ltd., Midway Oilfield Services Ltd. and G and W Oilfield Services Ltd. is now in the hands of a receiver. Why?
April 20, 1982

Because of the shutdown of the oil wells and the general depression in the oil industry.
There are hundreds of others, particularly throughout the heavy oil-producing area. These wells are very labour-intensive. They produce 20 to 30 barrels a day. This government with its buying policies would rather buy $40 a barrel oil from Venezuela and the OPEC countries and leave our oil shut in. These people are being forced to close their businesses and lay off people.
We all know of the number of rigs which have left this country; it has been cited many times. Between 235 and 240 oil drilling rigs have left Alberta and Saskatchewan to find work in the United States-in Oklahoma, Wyoming, Texas and other places. In addition, between 100 and 150 service rigs, each employing 40 to 50 people, are gone. It is like little factories being closed in western Canada. I wonder what the people of Ontario would say if they saw this happening before their eyes because of a deliberate government policy. It is a real tragedy that this is being allowed to happen in Canada.
Let us look at some other facts. This is what Bralorne Resources Limited said in its third quarter 1981 report:
The strong growth trend in our United States operations continued while Canadian operations struggled as drilling activity in the third quarter was down by more than 50 per cent from the same period last year. If anything, the decline recorded in the third quarter exceeded that of the previous quarter. ... As a result, the United States percentage of total revenues has increased from slightly more than 50 per cent in the first three quarters of 1980 to approximately 65 per cent in the same period this year ...
Reflecting our policy of increased United States involvement, more than 80 per cent of our 1981 plant expenditures have been on United States facilities.
[DOT]	(1620)
While United States expenditures this year have more than doubled, Canadian expenditures have been halved as a direct result of current pricing and market conditions.
Let us look at the Houston Business Journal, a very interesting item, Mr. Speaker. It is headlined "Canadian Connection: Energy, Money, Politics Blur Borders". It points out that since the passage of the National Energy Program $2.5 billion of Canadian investment capital has found its way into the United States and much of it into the area around Houston.
In the same paper there is a statement from a Mr. Joe Tondue. He is quoted as saying:
"Canadian money is moving in droves to Texas. 1 have joint ventures with three Canadian groups right now where they are paying all my costs and promotions in advance."
Then there is another man, Philip K. Sywden, who is quoted as saying:
"We have seen quite a bit of Canadian money because of our high profile in Western Canada."
He goes on:
Hundreds and hundreds of people who have invested left Canada and have invested in the United States. At least two dozen Canadian companies have opened up branch offices in the area around Houston.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I have another quote. It is from Energy Forum which substantiates the case that I am attempting to make. It says:
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
-investors have come to believe that Canada simply cannot be trusted ... The record shows that development of energy resources in Canada is falling off, the Canadian dollar is weaker, Canada's economic growth is also being retarded and jobs are being exported to the U.S. All this means a reduced standard of living in both countries (although less so for the U.S.) and a serious injury to a friendship unique between nations.
It goes on to say:
Joseph E. Seagram & Co. has already refused to repatriate upwards of $4 billion in investment capital to Canada because of the Canadian federal government's policies. This year more than 12 per cent of the oil and natural exploration gas in the U.S. will be produced by Canadian companies using workers and equipment that have shifted drilling to the U.S. and, if past experience is any indication, they will not return to Canada until the government alters course.
In short, the Ottawa policies are having the exact opposite effect of their stated purpose.
Mr. Speaker, we have capital, men, equipment, machines and expertise flowing south of the border. We need that investment capital here, we need that expertise here, we need the job opportunities here. We must stop that flow; indeed, we must reverse that flow of Canadian investment capital south of the border. We must keep that investment capital here in Canada, invest it in Canadian projects and in Canadian enterprises, so that we can preserve the kind of Canadian economic independence that so many people in this House talk about, but who will really not back it up with positive policies.
The fact of the matter is that even Mr. Gorse Howarth, our distinguished head of the Foreign Investment Review Agency, is quoted in an article in the Toronto Star of April 1, 1982 as saying:
Despite a dramatically high level of foreign ownership and control of Canadian industry, Canada has to drum up more business abroad if it wants to survive.
He talks about the need for additional investment capital in this country if we are going to be self-sufficient in energy and able to do those kinds of things which will provide a reasonable and decent standard of living for all Canadians, young and old included.
What about the consumer in all this, Mr. Speaker? We all naturally have to be concerned about the consumer, but the fact of the matter is that today, while our energy prices and our gasoline prices are on the increase, prices in the United States are on the decline. Ours are going up and theirs are going down. In the process, the consumer is being shafted.
Based on statistics which I have before me, the national average for the price of gasoline in December 1979 was $1.14 a gallon; that is the national average right across the country. As of March, 1982 it is exactly $2 a gallon; it has almost doubled in two years. That happened during a campaign which was to have promised cheap energy. As a matter of fact, the price for 1980 was to have been kept below 14 cents. We know that the prices have now doubled. So much for that promise as well. The consumer is indeed being ripped off.
Let us look at the producer. The farmers of Canada are now paying 60 cents a gallon for the diesel fuel that they burn in their tractors and in their combines. It has always been traditional and customary that the producers of food get some fair shake, some exemption, because they are not in a position to pass their additional costs along. The farmer pays 60 cents a

April 20, 1982
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
gallon when he fills up his tractor. That money goes into the federal government's coffers. I call that a massive federal government tax rip-off. It should be examined and the tax be reduced. If we are going to pursue a cheap food policy as this government has said, the farmers of Canada must get a break, and a break they should receive.
What about natural gas prices? They too have doubled. In western Canada we use natural gas to heat our homes and we have seen a doubling in the price of our fuel bill. Natural gas has a direct impact on the price of fertilizer. Our fertilizer prices are up by $25 to $40 a ton, and that will increase to about $70 a ton at the end of the energy pricing agreement, because of the increase in the price of natural gas. And the price increase in natural gas is composed, to the extent of 75 per cent or 80 per cent, of federal government taxes.
There you have it, Mr. Speaker. No one has benefited from the National Energy Program-not the people who work in the industry, the people who own the industry or the people who consume the product. It has been an absolute and total disaster and an absolute and total failure; and, above all, it has been a bureaucratic nightmare, as my colleague from Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) pointed out in his original remarks. The fact of the matter is that the regulations, the myriad of forms and the unwieldy discretionary powers that are given into the hands of bureaucrats in terms of administering this particular program will make it absolutely nightmarish and nothing more than confusion and frustration.
When this bill was introduced by the Minister of Energy Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), he called it the climax of all the measures having to do with Canadianization. He talked about it being the ultimate in achieving all of those things that unanimously Canadians had endorsed during the election campaign of 1980 and continue to endorse.
All I have to say to you, Mr. Speaker, is that if that is the case why are we experiencing the massive exodus of men, equipment, machines and capital out of this country? Why are we experiencing the bankruptcies, the foreclosures, the shutting downs, the dislocation of employees? Why are we experiencing this frustration, this sense of alienation in western Canada? It is because it is seen that the National Energy Program is a direct attack upon the resources of western Canada. It is not achieving the goal for which it was intended. It is destroying a once proud and once viable Canadian energy industry.
This hodge-podge, bureaucratic nightmare that is supported by the NDP is going to continue to frustrate and destroy until it is withdrawn or fundamentally changed. Hopefully, with the common sense and good, sound judgment of Canadians across this country, we may have to wait only a year or 18 months for an election. I am sure that the resourcefulness and the enterprising spirit of western Canadians will be able to live it through somehow until we can turf out this outfit, that Liberal rump over there. If we can turf them out at the same time, we can get on with the job of building a Canada that is based on equal opportunities. We want to have a Canada in which there is fairness and equity in all regions and for all individuals, a Canada which will be governed equally from region to region
rather than attacked at one end and favoured at the other. If we can survive until those changes are put into effect-and I am sure we can-there will certainly be better days ahead.
However, for the time being we have no choice but to condemn this measure because of the government's record in the past. We have no hope that this minister will change and see that he is out in his reckoning. This government is simply determined to forge on a course which has been destructive, and all we can do is point out, on behalf of our constituents and people in the industry, the fallacy of this particular measure. We hope there will be better days ahead, and I am sure there will be because they cannot get much worse than they are at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in opposition to Bill C-104 principally because quite unnecessarily it would give about $6.5 billion to the people in Canada and elsewhere who need it the least and will do the least good with it. The plan over the next five years is to give $6.5 billion to the private oil companies which already have received far too much by way of subsidy from Canadian working people. In this I am speaking particularly for the people of Spadina. There are no oil wells in Spadina, but there certainly are places at which the oil companies are making money. They get their money from the thousands of working people in Spadina and in the rest of the country. Those are the people who are subsidizing the oil companies.
Over the last few years oil companies have committed obvious rip-offs. The previous speaker whined about companies being accused of ripping off, but it has been established by the Bertrand inquiry that oil companies were guilty of ripping off about $12 billion from the Canadian public through rigging the prices of oil products.
The Conservatives support that.

Of course. The Conservatives support that as heartily as the Liberals. Over about 15 years oil companies ripped off at least $12 billion and, according to the Bertrand inquiry, they are continuing to do the same thing. These are the companies we are now asked to entrust with another $6.5 billion. These are the industries which boosted their assets from about $14.5 billion in 1973 to $54.5 billion in 1980. In seven years those assets multiplied four times, and the industry is complaining that multiplying assets four times in seven years is not enough.
In spite of the whining we hear from the far right in this House, according to government estimates, in general the prices and tax policies have provided the industry with the cash flow necessary to finance its expenditures. This means that the oil consumer and the Canadian taxpayer have financed virtually all of the substantial expansion of this industry. This continued into last year. During the first six months of 1981 a few oil companies took over several other oil companies, to the tune of $5 billion. That was only half a year's worth. At the
April 20, 1982

end of that about 70 per cent of the industry was still foreign owned and 70 per cent was still foreign controlled. So much for the Canadianization program of this government.
The government has not seriously tried to put the industry under the control of the Canadian people. It has simply sought to benefit a few individual Canadians by having Canadians buy the industry a second time after it had subsidized the industry over the past decades. The government has allowed the purchase of Canadian control by using Canadians' money against themselves. Having allowed all this to happen at the hands of foreign owners, the government would now like to force Canadian workers to pay for the industry again in order to buy it back. This is not for Canadian workers who are paying the taxes, but it is to buy the industry back for some hungry Canadian entrepreneurs who would like to be little local Rockefellers.
For example, over the past four years the tax concessions to this sector were worth a total of about $13 billion, yet during those years the industry paid only about $5 billion in taxes. In other words, the industry received back better than two dollars for every one dollar it paid in taxes. That is the kind of subsidy the industry has been given by all the other Canadians who are not owners of the oil industry.
The effective tax rate proposed for the oil industry would be about 10 per cent; that is to say, 36 per cent but down to 10 per cent after we knock off all the gifts the government has been giving and will give increasingly to oil companies. This compares with the married taxpayer with two children and an income of $25,000 who has to pay 18 per cent. If a company earns several billion or several million, it pays only 10 per cent in reality, and the people to the extreme right are complaining that oil companies are being hard done by.
We are complaining that the people are being hard done by.

If the tax concessions were ended, the federal government would be about $4 billion better off, and we could do something useful with that money for the people of Canada. We could restore the nearly $1.5 billion which was just chopped out of the annual payments from the federal government to the provinces. We could extend aid to post-secondary education, which is less in this country than it is in the countries with which we have to compete industrially. We could extend the daycare, which certain cabinet ministers keep promising every couple of months they will do but do not do it. We could extend pensions, which they also promise every two or three months to do without doing it. Those would be real benefits to the working people of Canada, but we do not get them because they are carted away by multinational oil companies.
There is another way of reckoning what has happened. In the year 1979 alone, for example, tax revenues from the petroleum industry forgone-that is, tax gifts to the petroleum industry-totalled $3.4 billion, but the industry's taxes amounted to only $1.4 billion. In other words, in that one year
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
all the other taxpayers of Canada were required to subsidize the oil companies to the tune of $2 billion.
That is Conservative policy too.

That is Conservative policy and Liberal policy. The Conservatives preach it; the Liberals practice it. The fact is that this is being continued and, as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said a couple of years ago in Toronto:
It is true we have imposed new taxes on the oil industry ... There have been complaints about this by the oil companies since the budget was brought down. But I can honestly say that their position will be no worse in 1981 than it was in 1979, perhaps even better.
He should know. Past tax gifts to corporations have given them far more than they needed. For example, the $2 billion we gave them a couple of years ago-and this is continuing- was not enough to induce them, according to my hon. friends to the right, to go on drilling for oil. My hon. friends would like us to give them $4 billion or $10 billion and then beg them to come back. In fact, there is no reason to suppose that that will get us any more oil, even if it is more oil that we need.
The government's proposal is that for every dollar the oil companies put up in most cases in Canada, the taxpayer would put up $4; but the taxpayer would get only 25 per cent equity in return. It is the only kind of investment where the major investor gets only a trifling equity and a trifling return.
The maximum benefit for a Canadian-owned company would be 93 cents on the dollar, and even for a multinational company the maximum benefit has risen, so that instead of paying 37 cents on the dollar it will now only have to pay 28 cents. All the rest is paid by the working people of this country.
That could only happen in Canada.

They simply do not need it, Mr. Speaker. They will take it if we give it to them. If we are stupid enough to let them, they will take it away. Countries like Norway do not give it at that rate. Norway will take up to 70 per cent interest in any block of land that it does not already hold if the oil companies find oil on it. That is because the oil belongs to the people of Norway. In Mexico the oil industry has been nationalized for over 40 years and now we see that country moving ahead.
Only a year ago the minister said that "this regime is more favourable to foreign investment than virtually any other country in the world." In that he is stating the truth, or perhaps he is even understating it. In Canada, the return to a taxable foreign company would be 27.7 per cent; to a Canadian company that is taxable it would be 29.7 per cent and to a Canadian company that is not taxable it would be 26.9 per cent. The lowest return on any of these would be that 26.9 per cent. In Norway it is only 18.3 per cent and in the United Kingdom it is 24.4 per cent.
We hear tear-jerking stories about the poor oil rig owners having to take their rigs down to Oklahoma. In Canada they
