Petroleum Incentives Program Act
were going to get 26.9 per cent so they went to Oklahoma where they will get only 21.6 per cent!
Oh, oh!
Nonsense. Get your facts straight. Tell the truth for a change.
They are going to get almost 6 per cent less in Oklahoma, but supposedly if we gave them more in Canada they would come back.
Oh, oh!

The jackals to my right have not told us how much more we would have to give them to bring them back to Canada. The fact is that these companies have now so much cash flow-more than they find it worth using for this country's development of oil-
Complete lies.

-that they will probably begin doing what they have already done in the United States. Since they have 30 per cent of the revenue in this country now, they will probably begin doing what they are doing in the United States and unfairly start buying into other industries outside the energy field.
Where do you get that stuff? In fairy tales?

Not only were all these tax subsidies given but there is another kind of subsidy that the working people of this country have been giving the oil companies for many years. Although the oil companies do not have any wells in Spadina, they have something more valuable-their head offices. Many of the people in Spadina built those head offices and banks that are the blood brothers of the oil companies-if they have any blood.
There are about 20,000 or 25,000 people who clean buildings in downtown Toronto-the oil companies and other head offices. These are mostly immigrant Portuguese housewives who spend about five and a half hours in the evening, five nights a week, cleaning those buildings. If they are lucky, after their husbands get home from their construction work they leave their families and go out to clean the buildings, coming home after eleven o'clock.
I have seen some of the conditions under which they work. As a representative of the board of health several years ago, I was called down to look into a dispute. The women were being forced to use stinking, used garbage bags that had been filled and emptied the night before. They were being told to reuse them because the contract cleaning company was too cheap to buy more bags. These women earn the minimum wage or, if they are lucky, 10 or 20 cents above.
There are also probably around 5,000 hospital workers in the Spadina area. We will not have up-to-date figures until the government releases the result of last year's census. There are probably another 10,000 restaurant and entertainment workers. I am not talking about the highly paid singers but about the people who keep the establishments going. Then there are
about 10,000 workers in the clothing and other manufacturing trades in Spadina. This is without the taxi drivers, the caretakers, the file clerks and servicemen of all kinds. There would be about 50,000 of these workers, almost all non-unionized and almost all on very low pay. Toronto has the lowest minimum wage of any city with over 500,000 population in Canada. In fact, the only other jurisdiction I know of with such a low minimum wage is the federal government, where it is $3.50 an hour.
If we estimate that these workers make on average about $4 per hour and work on average a 40-hour week, then in a year they earn in the range of $8,000. That is not much money on which to raise a family, especially with the housing and rental prices they have to pay in Toronto.
But there is more to it, Mr. Speaker. The work they do as cleaners is recognized at least in one part of the federal jurisdiction, the CBC where there is a union, as being worth $6.50 an hour. So most of these workers are in fact working for about $2.50 less than the fair wage. Add to that the fact that in a year they have to pay about $200 in taxes, about $250 in transit fares and probably $3,500 or $4,000 for daycare, and it all adds up. They may not be able to pay that much for daycare and sometimes what they get is rotten care. I am talking about the value of the work that is done to look after a kid or the value of the work that has to be done later done to repair the damage when the kid is not properly looked after, when his parents have to work.
Altogether these workers are subsidizing their employers to the extent of about $9,000 per year if you consider what they are paid, subtracted from the value of their work and the cost to them of performing their work. Instead of being paid $8,000 they ought to be paid about $17,000 if you calculate it on the basis of a low union wage, the cost of looking after their children, the cost of getting to work and taxes. The average person there is subsidizing these companies by about $9,000 per year, and there are about 50,000 of them. That makes a subsidy of about $450 million which the banks, oil companies and some of their confreres are taking away from the working people in downtown Toronto.
Senator Olson, who of course does not undertake to meet workers and ask for their vote, is appointed to be in charge of economic development and he says these are unproductive workers. A few weeks ago he said we are going to get rid of these industries, we are going to stop propping up unproductive industries such as the clothing industry and so on. What he means is that these workers are low paid, and therefore he calls them unproductive. In fact, these workers are subsidizing his favourite, the oil industry. If there is anything which should be phased out on the basis of productivity or on the basis of who is subsidizing whom, it is not the clothing workers, building cleaners or restaurant workers; it is the oil companies. The only reason in the practical sense why the oil companies
April 20, 1982

continue to receive such gifts from the federal government, whether it is Liberal or Conservative, is that they are so reliable in their gifts at election time.
How much did you get from the labour unions?
For example, in just one year the major companies gave $388,166 to the Conservative Party. They gave $332,942 to the Liberal party.
They protect themselves on both sides of the House.
Of course. They do not know which one will win the election-
We know you won't.

-but they know whichever one it is, it will give them the taxpayers' money. These people attempted to do the usual thing in Spadina last summer, but not all the money of the oil companies and the banks could elect Jim Coutts in Spadina, last summer or any other summer.
You were elected by a minority.

The fact is that the working people of this country are fed up with subsidizing the banks, the oil companies, the Tories and the Liberals. Our position is getting more and more support. What we are saying is, do not give that $6.5 billion to the private oil companies. If that money is going to be spent in the oil business by Canadian taxpayers, it should be to take control of companies like Imperial Oil. It would be much better to have the major oil companies in Canada controlled by Canada's elected representatives than to have it controlled by the unelected representatives such as Rockefeller.
With that money we could put control of the oil industry in the hands of the Canadian people, not in the hands of the buddies of the Conservatives or Liberals who happen to be the chief shareholders of Nova, Dome, Imperial and companies like that. We could then bring the revenue back to the people from whom it originally came-the building cleaners, taxi drivers, restaurant workers, construction workers and school teachers, the people who produced that $6.5 billion in taxes. They need it for health care, which this government is helping to destroy, and which the Conservative Party would probably destroy a little faster if it had the chance. The people need it for education, which again this government is destroying, as is the Conservative government in Ontario. They need it to institute daycare for the children of working parents, which is becoming a widespread need in this country as more and more families are forced to have two breadwinners. They need it in order to provide low rental housing, which the owners of the very large development companies refuse to provide.
This $6.5 billion comes from the ordinary working people of Canada. It should be spent on their behalf, not on behalf of the
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
Gallaghers, the Rockefellers, the Blairs, and the get-rich-quick boys who would like to have private ownership paid for by the public. It is public money, it should be under public control and benefit the public.

speechtext: It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 40, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert)-Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements-Amount of transfers to provinces; the hon. member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges)- Government Annuities-Yield to purchasers, (b) Request that government redeem low yielding annuities; the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson)-Pipelines-Delay in construction of Alaska Gas Pipeline, (b) Construction guarantees.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-104, respecting petroleum incentives and Canadian ownership and control determination and to amend the Foreign Investment Review Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation.

Mr. Speaker, once again it is my privilege, or my lot, to follow one of my friends on the left. We sometimes call these people socialists, but this was a Marxist-Leninist speech by the hon. member. He told us the workers have no control in this country, and the downtrodden are being abused by Liberals, Conservatives and free enterprisers. I have never been one to make apologies for free enterprise and enlightened capitalism, but I would like to ask the hon. member, who just said the people of Canada are waking up and becoming wise to all the schemes that the Liberals and Conservatives have imposed on them, why it is that in the most recent election in Newfoundland the NDP popular vote dropped from 10 per cent to 3.5 per cent?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
The people got wise.

April 20, 1982
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
Now, there is a really rich province. There are a lot of workers there who are really rich, yet the NDP popular vote dropped to 3.5 per cent.
What about Manitoba?

These people only enjoy support in areas where there are entrepreneurs, the people that have built this country, that they can leech off of. That is why they have one member from Newfoundland, and that is why they are going to lose the Saskatchewan election a week from now.
Oh, oh!

Just listen to them. How delightful; if you do not see them, you hear them! What nonsense. Imagine, the cleaning women employed by the multinational oil companies in Toronto are working at a minimum wage. They are all immigrant women and working at the minimum wage. The cleaning women who work for the CBC are paid three times as much as the people working for the oil companies. He has ignored the fact that the CBC gets close to $1 billion of taxpayers' subsidy every year. He talks about subsidies to the oil companies; what about the subsidies to the CBC?
We have a news team which comes on every night after the news on "The Journal", two women who have been there for ten months and they now need a five-month rest. This is exciting, this is wonderful. The hon. member wants to have complete control of every resource company in Canada so that in some magical way they can redistribute the wealth generated by their activities. The question is, who is going to carry out the activity? I would like to ask the hon. member how much control he exercised over Petro-Canada. We own it, it is ours whether we like it or not, and I would like to know how much control he exercised over it when it bought Petrofina for $1.5 billion. We know Imperial Oil would not have bought it. If Imperial Oil had, it would not have bought a single barrel of new oil. Imperial Oil would not have created a single new job or new enterprise of any kind because it was already in existence.
The hon. member tells us that the oil companies are going to earn $6.5 billion over the next five years.
Oh, oh!
It was just sold out yesterday by your friends in Victoria. Ask them.

Mr. Speaker, is it not delightful to get under the skin of the members of the little red rump of the Liberals? The hon. member is talking about the multinationals, the woodworkers and the oil workers. I do not hear the oil workers who are working complaining. I do not hear them at all. I do not hear them talking about multinational unions and the control that American unions exercise over the workers in this country, or about the disunity that exists. I do not hear these great spokesmen of the workers and the downtrodden talking about that.
Let me return to the $6.5 billion which the multinational oil companies are going to be earning over the next five years. We know, and the statistics bear this out, that the price of a litre or of a gallon of oil is broken down in a way where the commercial value of the product is roughly 32 per cent of the pump price. This means that if the oil companies earn $6.5 billion over the next five years, the federal and provincial governments will earn $13 billion. That is my arithmetic.
It is going back to the oil companies.

If the hon. member would sit down and figure it out, he would realize that. Oil companies have to drill for oil, bring it to the surface, they have to refine it, they have to load it on to trucks after refining and haul it to service stations. No matter what day the oil reaches the gas station, the service station operator has to be there whether it is seven o'clock in the morning, eight o'clock in the morning or whatever. The operator puts it in your car and washes your windshield. All of this is done for about 16 cents per litre.
The federal government and the provincial government are earning from the same activity 26 cents a litre. But they get this 26 cents without doing a thing. Not only that, there is a margin of profit in the 16 cents which the oil companies receive from each litre. The government will tell them how to invest and reinvest the small margin of profit that is left. What more controls do Canadians need? Why is it that we have to invest another $100 billion of taxpayers' money to attain the same kind of control that we already have?
Since visiting my constituency I am now in the process of putting together a private member's bill which will make it mandatory under the products labelling act that the price be broken down of a consumer product which is heavily controlled by governments and shown on the package. After all, the components of a product have to be listed on the package, and must be done in both official languages. Why should the price of gasoline not be broken down? It should be shown that 16 cents a litre is the commercial value, that the provinces keep 13 cents or 14 cents for themselves for doing nothing and the federal government keeps 12 cents for itself for doing nothing.
Why should we not list the commercial cost of a bottle of rum? A bottle of rum imported from Jamaica costs roughly $3.10. That rum is sold in liquor stores for $19 or $20. Why should consumers not know what their actual tax bill is?
Workers pay for this tax. So do people who put gasoline in their cars to drive to work. What about the farmers who put gasoline and diesel fuel into their tractors and their cars as part of their job of producing food which is nutritious and plentiful? Why should consumers not know what the government is already up to? That is why I am putting together this private member's bill. I recommend it to all members. If we had these kinds of requirements it would make very interesting reading and the people would know exactly where their money is going.
April 20, 1982

The National Energy Program was designed to achieve a 50 per cent or better Canadian ownership content. I have mentioned before that Canadian ownership content has to be defined. The socialists in this chamber have not yet done that. It means government ownership. There are no ifs, ands or buts about that. Canadian ownership would mean that purchase of shares in Petro-Canada or any other corporation would be restricted to Canadians only or that only wholly Canadian-owned companies could operate in Canada lands or in the oil patch. That would be Canadian ownership. But Bill C-48, which is the National Energy Program, is designed to do nothing else but give governments complete ownership of this important sector of our economy. The National Energy Program will not give us energy self-sufficiency by 1990.
Oil is not a tool of production, nor is energy, but you certainly need oil to grease the machine used for that production. We know the Marxist theory that the people have to have control of the tools of production. Labour produces wealth. Labour multiplied by the machine produces more wealth. The government has to have control and ownership of the machine. For the life of me I cannot believe that intelligent people here would tell us that all will be well as soon as we have, as this government or any other government has, even a Conservative government, control and ownership of all the tools of production.
Why is all not well in the Soviet Union or for that matter any other socialist country in the world? Governments own all the resources in socialist countries.
They cannot feed themselves.

Those are the countries that own all their agricultural lands. It is 63 years since the revolution in the Soviet Union, but the Soviet Union has had 63 consecutive crop failures. The gods must have been really angry at the people in the Soviet Union. Imagine, Mr. Speaker-they have had 63 consecutive crop failures! Those failures occurred immediately following the period when the Ukraine fed all of Europe. Then there was the revolution and 63 consecutive crop failures followed.
I suggest that there is something else at play. There is complete Russian ownership of the oil, of the energy sector, of the lumber industry and of the agricultural sector. In fact, in every other resource sector the Soviet Union has complete ownership. That is why the people in the Soviet Union are starving. That is why the Soviet Union has to import wheat from Canada and from the United States. The Soviet Union will not be importing wheat from Canada much longer if these fellows to my left have too much influence on those opposite. They have already asserted too much influence on them. They seem to believe that the state has to own the tool of production so that everything can be equitably redistributed without knowing whether or not people produce or contribute anything to the economy. We all know what the end effect of that kind of policy would be.
We are not here to make excuses for the multinational oil companies if they have been irresponsible. Some have. It is no one's fault but theirs because we have total control over them.
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
We tell them where to drill for oil. We tell them if they find any. It is very seldom they do. We tell them how much to recover, where to deliver it and how much to charge for it. We set the wellhead price, we set the pump price. We do all that. Why do we have to own it?
The government is acting with such indecent haste trying to get the bill through the House because we are already learning the effects of the National Energy Program. The longer it takes, the more people will become aware of what is happening, particularly when this monstrosity of a bill is in place. Approximately $6.5 billion of Canadian investment capital has left the country for the United States. We realize the effects that this will have on the poor workers of the United States. It has been given back to free enterprise. The people of the United States will be ripped off. In the short period of one year since the NEP was announced and parts of it implemented, there has been a decrease in the price of gasoline in the United States. But our prices are still increasing because, after all, we have ownership in Canada! With that $6.5 billion moved Canadian expertise, Canadian technology and Canadian jobs.
I should like to cite one example. Fort St. John is in my constituency-
Oh, oh!

If hon. members listened, they might learn something. The truth always hurts. It certainly hurts those people in the corner. The hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) should listen to what I am saying. I do not know why the people of that riding wanted to elect this man to the House of Commons rather than Jim Coutts who had the same theories as he. He wanted to nationalize the farming industry. He did not believe in private ownership of farms or private property. He wanted to do the same things as the hon. member for Spadina.
The Tories placed third in Spadina.

I do not know why the people of Spadina wanted the hon. member. At least Mr. Coutts would have had some influence on the other side. Perhaps he would have been able to do these things much faster. As we all know, Canadians will not stand for this radical alternative to a time-honoured system which has served our country well. This system has made us one of the leading industrial nations of the world and one of the most industrious and prosperous peoples of the world.
Returning to the effects of the National Energy Program in some communities, one of these communities is located in my constituency. The entire area of British Columbia which produces oil and natural gas is within my constituency. In Fort St. John and the general northeastern area of British Columbia a couple of years ago 120 oil and gas rigs were active. Each one of these rigs had roughly 60 to 65 jobs attached to it. As we all know, there were incredible spin-off effects on service industries. For example, there were mud

April 20, 1982
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
companies, machine shops, testing companies, water trucks which ran back and forth, welders and trucking companies which moved the rigs. All these spin-off effects have gone. Right now there are 18 rigs working in that entire area of British Columbia. In fact, a couple of years ago there were some Petro-Canada rigs working in northeastern British Columbia, but there are no such rigs working there now.
They have gone offshore.

They have gone to Senegal and to the North Sea; this is where Petro-Canada is active. Esso Canada is not active in Senegal or the North Sea. It is only active in Canada because multinational companies are active in these other areas and there is no way that Esso Canada can go there.
What are the effects of this massive downturn in the activities of this important industry? The effects are devastating. For example, there have been bankruptcies. We heard some statistics this morning, but specifically there was an increase in unemployment in Fort St. John to 160 per cent from the first three months of January, February and March of 1981 to the first three months of this year. A major car dealer has gone bankrupt. A lifetime of work was invested in this business which was once prosperous and doing well, and the dealer has gone into receivership. He responded to what he heard in the House of Commons a couple of years ago, namely a firm commitment by government that Canada would achieve energy self-sufficiency by 1990. The government indicated that this would require an investment of somewhere between $300 billion and $500 billion, and that all of us would have to use the entrepreneurial spirit for which we are famous to invent new ways to find energy.
My area responded; a lot happened. There was an increase in the number of hotel rooms in Fort St. John from 320 to 1,100 in two years. Now several of the major hotels, including a Holiday Inn, are in receivership. The good local people who invested in motels, coffee shops and machine shops are now trying to find ways to deduct their losses from income tax. This is difficult as they are not paying any income tax, since they have no income.
As I say, the effects are devastating. We will not achieve energy self-sufficiency by 1990. In fact, we will be importing more than 50 per cent of our requirements by 1990 if we proceed with the program. The best we could hope for is that world energy prices continue to decline and that the import compensation which is paid so that people can heat their homes will not be too onerous on us. When I say "onerous on us", I am talking about the government. Of course, the government cannot give anything away which it has not first taken from someone else. I am speaking more about those of us in the west, particularly in the provinces of British Columbia and Alberta, who are paying these import compensation charges, because we are the only "have" provinces in Canada; every other province is in the "have not" category.
It is utterly amazing to sit here in good conscience, knowing the effects of the NEP, assiduously and stubbornly pushing ahead with the scheme. If there were any light at the end of
the tunnel, if it were necessary to destroy in order to rebuild, I could understand it. As in other areas of the economy, if it were an attempt to rearrange the attitudes of people to make them more conscious of the realities of the modern world, I could understand it. But that is not the case.
We had a good industry. A good percentage of the industry was already Canadian. There is a great misconception that the oil sector is totally controlled by multinational companies. Although multinational companies have sometimes been very irresponsible in the arrangement of their corporate structures and the behaviour of their corporate bureaucrats in relation to small businessmen with whom they work in the oil patch, they have always known and understood that the best and most productive way to achieve new wealth and to get the job done is through private enterprise. That is why you do not see an oil rig company out there directly servicing an oil rig; they leave that to private enterprise.
Until a few years ago, when they had to react to certain legislation which was brought in by that socialist government on the other side, they always knew that the best way to sell gas and the best person to be the final chain in the link was an entrepreneur. That is why the service station operator is a private businessman. The oil companies knew that this was the best, most productive and efficient way to deliver oil and gas to the producer. The oil companies always knew that and it is unfortunate that this government does not understand it. Instead, this government wants to tear down this industry and replace it with some radical alternative which has never worked anywhere else in the world. It knows what the effects will be but it is so stubborn in its attempts to break the present system apart in order to try something which we all know will not work.
Socialism has never worked anywhere and those members to my left should know that. They can look anywhere in the world where there is a socialist or communist government and see that there are people starving, being deprived and experiencing shortages in the supply of important consumer goods. If those people can obtain some goods they must buy them in the black market and pay excessive prices for them.
When they are exploited they have to turn to something.

Those members know that people are exploited and workers are exploited by insensitive centralist, socialist government bureaucracies ten times more than workers who have a choice to work in one free enterprise establishment or another.
The answer is not for all Canadian workers to begin working for the Canadian government. In five years the government will not have enough money to take steps to regain its position in world markets-a position which provided a standard of living which was number three in the world and is now twelve or thirteen. The answer will not be found in government
April 20, 1982

ownership. The answer is in the return of the inspiration of the free spirit and the incentives required for individuals to invest in themselves and their country in order to restore in Canadians a confidence in their ability to produce. The first step towards that goal is to instil confidence in Canadians once again. Without that confidence I am very much afraid that we will have to continue to hope that the Americans will emerge from their dilemma and that their prosperity, which was based on these old principles, will once again spill over into our country.
The hon. member also indicated that in the last ten years the oil companies have increased their wealth by four times. What he neglected to say was that the government has increased its size tenfold during the same period. That is a clear indication of where we are heading, which is toward disaster unless we all screw up our courage. I am particularly looking for the backbenchers in the government to screw up their courage and say that enough is enough. They are representing ridings in the great provinces of Quebec and Ontario where unemployment is far greater than the national average. Businesses in those provinces which produced pipelines for the west, equipment for wells and tools used in the oil patch are going bankrupt because there is no demand. Let those Liberal backbenchers screw up their courage and stand up to the people who are determined to replace our time-honoured system with this radical alternative of government control and ownership, centralist control and socialism. Time is running out. It is time for us and for all Canadians to wake up and call an end to this incredible nonsense.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Dingwall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in this debate. It is interesting to note that the official opposition, the Conservative party of Canada, are opposed to providing moneys under the petroleum incentives program to the oil and gas industry in Canada. Similarly, it is interesting to note that the New Democratic Party of Canada is opposed to this particular piece of legislation as well.
Unfortunately, a number of events have taken place in the last twenty-four hours, particularly with respect to the words used by the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre). At best, I think it can be said that his remarks regarding the role of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) in providing a direction for Canadians and the government relating to our energy policy has not only been uncomplimentary but bordering on unparliamentary. He made reference to the "battle of the bells". He stated that he would have prevented that battle if he had been assured that this particular piece of legislation on the petroleum incentives program would be given quick passage. I do not wish to debate the substance of his remarks while that hon. member is not in the House, so I will simply refer him to the remarks made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources which were recorded in Hansard on March 1, 1982. I believe that clarifies beyond a shadow of a doubt what transpired between the minister and himself.
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
By objecting to this particular piece of legislation and voting against it, it is evident that the Conservatives are indicating to the oil and gas industry that they will not provide any incentives for exploration and development. I believe it is shameful that they seem to be speaking out of both sides of their mouths. While they say they support the oil and gas industry, when it comes to providing actual incentives they either do not take a position, or if they do, it is not a favourable one for the industry.
The hon. member for Calgary Centre talked about the goal of Canadianization and how he agreed with that goal. Unfortunately, he did not agree with the process for achieving Canadianization. I suggest to him that there is no easy process to accomplish the Canadianization goal. Canadianization has been talked about for many years in Canada. In order to achieve this we will have to go through some difficult times and address a number of concerns over a period of time.
The hon. member also took the opportunity to greatly criticize the officials of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. I call that criticism a very cheap shot and very unbecoming of a Member of Parliament. I think each hon. member of this House, regardless of on what side he or she may sit, should hold that hon. member in shame for such despicable and uncomplimentary remarks.
The hon. member for Calgary Centre also made a statement of the effect that there are too many forms to be filled out and too many regulations to be complied with. I suppose if the hon. member had his wish the Government of Canada would provide large sums of money to the oil and gas industry, in excess of a billion dollars, without any strings, conditions, rules or guidelines attached. I ask members of the House, is that responsible government? Inevitably it is not. Nor it is the intention of this government.
Of course, representing his party, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), that great mini-giant of the working class people of Canada, came to this chamber and said to the Parliament of Canada that he was very concerned that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources was not here while he was giving his speech. Therefore, he wanted to call for a quorum and he called for a quorum last night. Your Honour knows what happened when he called for the quorum. He and other hon. members in his party, each and every one, left the chamber.
Shame!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
It was suggested, not by me, that perhaps the reason for calling the quorum was that the hon. member had a more important engagement to attend and that this particular piece of legislation, as it affects energy in Canada, was not a priority with him or his party. I do not know if that is true, but I think the record should very clearly show that the NDP called a quorum. All its members vacated the House of Commons. A quorum was called, we had sufficient numbers,

April 20, 1982
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
and then we came back and resumed debate. That was shameful conduct on the part of the NDP and the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
I will not quote the hon. member, but the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway had the audacity to suggest that perhaps there was an intellectual-I use that term quite loosely-understanding between his party and the government of the province of Quebec, when he referred to Rene Levesque. Is that where the NDP stands? I ask that question quite sincerely.
We have made encouraging progress toward our goal of achieving at least 50 per cent Canadian ownership by 1990. In the past year, with the changes from foreign to Canadian control of such large companies as Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Limited, Aquitaine Company of Canada Limited and Petrofina of Canada Limited, foreign control declined by about 10.5 per cent to a level of approximately 67.2 per cent. At the same time, the level of foreign ownership of upstream production revenue was 65.5 per cent, a drop of 6.5 percentage points in one year.
While the purchases of foreign-owned oil companies are vital to the government's Canadianization plan; they are not the only means. This bill provides another means by which Canadians can take charge of their oil and gas industry.
There have been some concerns raised by hon. members of the official opposition that the energy legislation, and particularly the bill which is now before us, is discriminatory toward the oil and gas industry in the United States. However, I wish to lay on the record a quote of the former President of the United States, Richard Nixon, who told this House in no uncertain terms on April 14, 1972, that:
No self-respecting nation can or should accept the proposition that it should always be economically dependent upon any other nation. Let us recognize once and for all that the only basis for a sound and healthy relationship between our two proud peoples is to find a pattern of economic interaction which is beneficial to both our countries and which respects Canada's right to chart its own economic course.
I think that statement tells it all. Mr. Nixon made that statement ten years ago. However, I do not have to tell hon. members of this House that Canada still faces the situation whereby we are still dependent upon other nations. This is particularly true in the oil and gas industry.
The petroleum incentives program is a very positive program-
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: -which offers incentives to Canadians to participate in their own industry. I can understand why the New Democratic Party opposes this. It would perhaps prefer that depletion allowances continue for the multinational oil companies. Then members of that party would perhaps have an opportunity to sit on the board of directors of those companies. That is probably what they want.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Like Tommy Douglas.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: This petroleum incentives program is one which we believe will lead to increased Canadian control and less dependence on foreign ownership. Our intent, as emphasized in the National Energy Program, is to mobilize predominantly private Canadian investment in the oil and gas industry.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: MOTOR VEHICLE FUEL CONSUMPTION STANDARDS ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-107 respecting motor vehicle fuel consumption standards be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation.
He said: Mr. Speaker with the legislation before the House at the present time the government is acting on a longstanding commitment to Canadians to address the problem of heavy consumption of fuel by motor vehicles. This legislation, the Motor Vehicle Fuel Consumption Standards Act, was first promised in 1976. Since then, as hon. members know, the government has provided a voluntary program while work on drafting and refining the legislation was carried on by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Depart-
Fuel Consumption Standards
ment of Transport. During that time we have had an American model to consider but not to follow slavishly.
The National Energy Program recognized that transportation uses more oil than any other sector and that conservation efforts would be crucial to moderating that demand. By world standards we waste fuel in this country, so we need an effective program of managing consumption. That is what is stated in the following section of the National Energy Program:
In Canada, standards have been voluntary. However, it has become increasingly clear that the automobiles constructed to suit United States legislative standards do not necessarily reflect the realities of vehicle operation in the colder Canadian climate, nor do they take cognizance of the relation between Canadian fuel types, feedstocks and motor vehicle fuel requirements. As part of a general conservation and liquid fuels policy, Canada will develop its own standards.
This legislation comes to grips with a persistent headache amongst conservationists. We are all familiar with North America's love affair with the automobile and how extensive that torrid relationship has become. In Canada the use of automobiles is more than just whim or fancy. Our country's population is flung across an awesome latitude, and transportation is vital to our way of life.
Much has already been accomplished. One would have to be blind not to see the changes that have taken place in car size and horsepower in recent years. The problem is not so easily solved, however. People have to be shown the substitute fuels that exist and they have to be encouraged to ease up on the accelerator and to make trips count when they pull out of the laneway. They also need information that will enable them to choose vehicles that best suit their needs and resources.
This legislation will make that information available and give the government the ability to make sure the choices are as attractive as possible.
To illustrate the progress that has been achieved, let me give you a few statistics, Mr. Speaker. In 1978 we estimate that new passenger cars in Canada had an average fuel consumption of 11.5 litres per 100 kilometres. Last year that had dropped to 9.5 litres per 100 kilometres, and this year we expect it to be down to 8.5 litres. Such progress is encouraging but it is far from enough. We have to do much more to reduce motor vehicle consumption than we have been able to accomplish with this voluntary program so far. Why? Because last year Canadian consumption of motor gasoline amounted to a staggering 225 million barrels.
I hardly need to remind anyone in this chamber of how important this bill is to our energy program. Throughout the NEP the effort to enhance both supply and conservation is evident. Here we are adopting yet another method to cut into oil imports and preserve for as long as we can the petroleum resources available to us. The transportation sector represents a staggering consumption of fuel. There were approximately seven million private cars on the road in Canada in 1980. They burned somewhere between 18 and 19 billion litres of gasoline travelling an estimated 112 billion kilometres. These statistics do not include trucks or cars in commercial use.

April 20, 1982
Fuel Consumption Standards
[ Translation]
More oil is required in this transportation sector than in any other, and although other fuels such as propane can be substituted for gasoline, this is not sufficient, at least not in the short term. Once again, we must save energy. Since substitutes are known, in abundant supply and ready for immediate use, it is the National Energy Program's aim to provide for efficient management of the demand for oil products in this sector. We shall be able to stabilize, and even reduce, the demand for oil products to a considerable extent through the proposed legislation on motor vehicle fuel consumption standards which is aimed at saving our energy resources. This additional authority would make existing voluntary guidelines for fuel consumption standards official and would give force of law to compulsory standards, should they prove to be desirable or necessary in the future. There are already signs of change in this sector, one example being the installation of relatively inexpensive aerodynamic deflectors on tractor-trailers, which help cut down on fuel consumption.
Carpool programs appear to be spreading, and are another way of reducing our transportation fuel requirements. However, not only the drivers' attitude must be changed. Driving itself must be rethought and revolutionized. This bill is therefore proposing a program that takes into account Canadian conditions and requirements on the basis of which the automobile industry will design and manufacture the cars of this decade. In 1975, the American government adopted legislation that set fuel consumption standards for cars. It is up to the manufacturers and importers to ensure that average consumption, weighted by the number of cars sold each year, meets annual standards. Since these standards are becoming increasingly stricter, the industry has been obliged to change the design of North American cars. Increasingly, however, cars manufactured to U.S. standards do not allow for the differences in climate and fuel encountered in Canada. Because of our energy policy, we need a made-in-Canada program. The bill on motor vehicle fuel consumption standards will authorize the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to continue the voluntary fuel consumption program.
The first part of the Act provides that a fuel consumption number will be given to each vehicle sold in Canada. The numbers will be used on information stickers for each vehicle and also to provide data for the Transport Canada transportation fuel consumption guide. The same figures will also be used by the Minister of Transport to calculate the fuel consumption of vehicles sold by manufacturers in Canada.
The vehicle categories covered by the legislation are to be general. For instance, private cars will form one category. The present voluntary program sets average motor vehicle fuel consumption standards for a company for every year up to 1985. Companies can reduce fuel consumption by selling more energy-saving cars or by refining each model in this respect at the design stage.
The government has decided that the program will remain voluntary unless companies fail to co-operate.

So as to hammer the point home, the authority to set standards and impose penalties is contained in the act. But the government does not intend that these provisions should be proclaimed. Just having written these sections into the law we hope will be enough to accomplish our goals.
We want detailed information for the consumer and for the government. We want to demonstrate to everyone, manufacturers, consumers, and the world that we are truly committed to saving scarce oil supplies and we want to be in a strong position to negotiate with the industry on voluntary standards. Obviously if we cannot achieve all of that without using the legal clout this offers us, we will resort to that approach. But for now the practice of setting voluntary fuel consumption standards will continue along with an improved flow of information.
The primary beneficiary here is not in fact the government but the consumer. We expect automobile manufacturers and dealers to display prominently energy consumption ratings and give the consumer the chance to make intelligent, informed decisions when in the vehicle marketplace. The government will compile the data to monitor the accuracy of the ratings and the progress we are making in getting more kilometres out of every drop of fuel.
We can also get a better idea of what is happening by way of research and how the new technology is performing. Such information is crucial to developing government policy. As the situation stands now we cannot be sure such complete information will be supplied. The consumer will also benefit by having the attention of automobile manufacturers focused on Canadian needs and conditions and on our supplies of gasoline or alternative fuels. Nothing in this bill should cause undue hardship to the industry, which we all know is hard pressed these days. We are really asking for very little additional information beyond what the industry now supplies. This act merely ensures that the information will in fact be forthcoming. The expense will be minor and the benefits potentially great. What it will do is to give us some data and some measurement directly related to the real world that Canadian motorists face. We have to find ways of looking for data which is relevant to the Canadian climate, which we all know has a mean temperature all its own.
If fuel consumption testing does not yield results which are translated into actual fuel consumption when cars and trucks are put into use on streets and highways, it is not of much use. The government needs to be sure it is getting complete and precise information if it is to verify for the consumer the numbers which manufacturers are turning out. We need this legislation to get that data. We also need a not so subtle means of encouraging automobile manufacturers to look at alternative fuels.
April 20, 1982

Again, this legislation focuses attention on the need to reduce fuel consumption in the face of rising prices and increasingly uncertain supplies. Obviously, one solution is using a different fuel. Hon. members will recall that the government has already taken some steps. We have offered grants of $400 under the propane vehicle grant program for those converting their farm or commercial vehicles to a propane fuel system or purchasing such vehicles new. Our target is 100,000 propane-powered vehicles by 1985. Since the program started last June we have received about 2,500 applications for grants. So far, about 3,650 vehicles have been accepted as eligible to receive the $400. That represents a saving of about 955 barrels a day of oil which would otherwise have been consumed as gasoline by these vehicles. The program has dispensed $1,460,800 so far. But it is more than just our grant program that makes propane gas an attractive alternative for motorists. Propane also offers a fuel that is significantly lower in price than conventional gasoline.
We have as well offered contributions to those willing to convert vehicles to compressed natural gas and help us demonstrate, in actual Canadian driving conditions, the value and versatility of this fuel. We are offering $600 contributions to those willling to undertake the conversion and to commit themselves to report back to us on what improvements they enjoyed in fuel consumption as a result.
The government has promised to hold the price of natural gas below that of oil as far as is possible, and that price differential as well should make compressed natural gas attractive as an alternative fuel. There are already more than
350,000	vehicles in the world operating on compressed natural gas, but we in Canada have little experience with the fuel, the hardware to make use of it or the results that can be achieved by making the switch. Our program started only in January, so it is a little early to judge any statistical results. However, we do know that we have natural gas in abundance and that as a fuel, it is less environmentally hazardous than conventional gasoline or diesel fuel.
We want transport fuel consumption in transport brought down. The transport sector is eating up too much of our limited supplies and we want to be in a position to achieve further improvements if this gentle approach does not work. I am sure that it will work because I know the automotive industry is as interested as the rest of us are in fuel consumption and energy self-sufficiency. If 1 needed any reassurance of that, I got it earlier this year when 1 met with the Motor Vehicle Manufacturers' Association. We all showed a great willingness to co-operate at that gathering.
As with other pieces of legislation being put before Parliament this spring, this bill is a means of formalizing the National Energy Program of October, 1980. It is just as important as all of the others, perhaps more so, since it addresses the crucial issue of conservation, the area where the actions of every citizen can mean so much in terms of saving fuel and buying
Fuel Consumption Standards
us time against the day, however distant, when oil wells everywhere run dry.

subtopic: MOTOR VEHICLE FUEL CONSUMPTION STANDARDS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to lead off the debate for the opposition on Bill C-107 respecting motor vehicle fuel consumption standards. If the minister was serious in some of the comments he has just made, I think it would be very sad indeed. He talked about the importance of conserving gas and that the responsibility of Canadian citizens was to ease back on the gas pedal and to conserve, conserve and conserve. Yet when we come into the House for a vote or a series of votes, we see lining up outside the House-it happened at question period today-a series of limousines, each one belonging to a cabinet minister. Every limousine's engine is kept running waiting for the cabinet minister to come out from the vote or to come out from question period.
One evening I made a point of counting the number of limousines with engines running. It was an evening when five votes took place. This took about an hour. Fourteen limousines were outside the House of Commons with their engines idling during the whole period. They were being kept warm for the privileged bunch over there.
The minister tells us that we have to conserve. It is the same old double standard that we hear around here on everything else. We hear that everybody must tighten his or her belt, except for them. We hear that everybody must conserve, except them. If the minister wanted to do something serious, the first thing he should do after this debate would be to go back to his office, dictate a memo to every member of the cabinet and to every other person who has a chauffeur driven car directing them to turn off the engines when not in use and thus conserve energy. Fourteen cars idling for an hour outside the House of Commons burns up an awful lot of gas. How do you expect the Canadian public to accept what the minister says about conservation when that kind of nonsense goes on here every day when the House is sitting?
In 1976 Canada implemented voluntary fuel efficiency standards for automobiles. Likewise in 1976 the government promised to bring forward legislation to put these standards into law. Well, we have finally seen that done. But it took six years after the government made that promise.
The government has never had to pass any of these efficiency standards into law. The government has been able to rely on the powerful American legislation. More important-and the minister realizes it today, and if he were up front with the Canadian people he would admit it-if he passed some regulations concerning fuel consumption for automobiles it would certainly be the tail wagging the dog because we have a North American auto industry and not a Canadian auto industry, so the minister must follow the regulations of the United States.
This is really a phony bill when one thinks about it. The smartest thing for the minister to do would be for him to say that yes, we have to label the cars here in Canada. It is being done now. All the ads reveal fuel consumption. But the simple

April 20, 1982
Fuel Consumption Standards
thing to do would be to follow the lead taken by the environmental protection agency and to co-operate with it and the two levels of government. That would make a lot more sense than going on with this phony bill which says, "We are going to pass the legislation but we are really not going to put it into force unless you misbehave, auto industry". I guess that is a form of blackmail.
We know the Canadian auto market is too small for us to be dictating to the American scene. In the past we have voluntarily formulated standards which are identical to those in the United States. That makes sense. This bill respecting motor vehicle fuel consumption standards continues the conceit of the federal government, except for a new twist. We all remember the former energy minister, Mr. Alastair Gillespie. He pretended that there were standards when there were none. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) now proposes to implement legislation to create standards, but then he pretends he has no real authority to do anything about it. He is not going to have the bill proclaimed. So we are still doing the same thing. The minister just wants to make it appear that he is being the big tough guy, that he will clamp down on the auto people and will make them toe the line.
The minister said that if the voluntary standards fail to work he would bring in compulsory standards and have the bill proclaimed. But this gives the government the authority to set a fuel consumption standard which the industry must meet. There is no mention at all in the bill of voluntary standards. There are really only two ways the government can implement voluntary standards under this bill. The first would be to set the standards by one regulation; the second would be to exempt everyone from them. Perhaps a third would be to set no standards at all. Really nothing at all has changed from Mr. Gillespie's day. What we have is a big facade. The minister is trying to impress the Canadian people with what he is doing, but he is not doing anything different from what has been done until now. The minister is attempting to drag some information out of the auto industry which heretofore he was unable to obtain. Is it because the auto industry would not produce it. I am not sure why he is doing it.
If we take a look at the American legislation, we will see that in 1973 the environmental protection agency initiated a voluntary fuel efficiency labelling program south of the border. In 1975 it passed amendments to the motor vehicle information cost saving in the United States which stipulated the actual fuel economy standard to be reached for each auto manufacturer for 1978 to 1980 and for 1985. Definite goals were set for the manufacturers. The 1981 to 1984 standards could be set by the secretary. Also they stipulated the means by which labels indicating fuel efficiency should be fixed to automobiles, and that EPA must in fact publish a book listing all efficiency ratings, which book must be available at all auto dealers for the benefit of consumers.
The efficiency testing program is a second aspect of the auto emissions testing program. It is interesting to note that the Americans ran their testing program in California. The minister alluded to the fact that their standards may not be
realistic for our climate. I agree with him, but he should remember that the Americans have just as severe a climate as ours in some parts of their country. There should be cooperation between the two levels of government in setting those standards. There should also be co-operation in testing because we desperately need research and development in Canada.
In reaching some of the levels about which the minister was talking, co-operation should take place between Americans and Canadians. After all, we are dealing with the North American car market, not just the Canadian market. As the minister said, the testing may be somewhat unrealistic, but I think this can be straightened out with the Americans and with auto manufacturers. In fact we do not need this bill which really does nothing; it does not have much teeth in it. I know it includes a fine of $1 million or five years in jail, but I would be interested to find out who would have to serve the sentence if the law as laid down by the minister was broken.
We are talking about no change at all. The bill is phony. As it does in many instances, the government is using a club to try to achieve goals which have already been set. As a matter of fact, the auto industry is moving toward the standards. For example, at present standards require that the new car fleets of each company average no more than 10.7 litres per 100 kilometres in 1981, which for the benefit of the hon. member for Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley) 26.4 miles per gallon, and that it improve to 8.6 litres per 100 kilometres by 1985, which is 33 miles per gallon. As the minister said, naturally companies can improve on these standards. I think many of them are. There are a number of reasons the auto industry is improving on that. First it is the competition with which the industry is faced. For far too long the governments of Canada and the United States have fooled their people. They had phony levels for the price of fuel which maintained the love affair of North Americans with big cars. The North American auto industry kept turning out these large cars because the governments were misleading people into thinking that gas prices would be kept down and that they could continue driving large cars. Now that the competition is here and now that prices have risen, naturally the auto industry will try to compete with some of the more fuel efficient automobiles we see coming into the country. They are making a move toward improving the mileage of their cars.
The minister talked about setting regulations so that people conserve gas, yet his own department brags about how consumption has gone down recently. Everyone knows why. It is because all levels of government are involved in the "big tax grab" and there are rapid increases in the cost of fuel, which in itself will guarantee less driving as people cannot afford to drive like they used to. They are not piling into their cars for Sunday drives, bumper to bumper, to see their friends in the country. This is not happening anymore because they cannot afford it, so consumption has dropped rather drastically.
The minister said that the government would carry on with the voluntary sector and that in fact it would not proclaim this act unless the industry stepped out of line. It is another slam at
April 20, 1982

the auto industry which is having an extremely difficult time now. There are thousands of lay-offs in the auto parts manufacturing industry and in the auto industry itself. Also, thousands of lay-offs from spin-offs linked directly to the industry are being experienced, especially in Ontario and Quebec. This is just another threat of this big government. It is telling the industry what to do, how to do it and, if it is not done, that it will be given a $1 million fine and plunked in jail for five years.
As a matter of fact I find one section of the proposed act somewhat interesting. I am referring to the one which allows the minister to take a car, or a component of a car, so that he can tear it apart to see what makes it run. Nowhere in the bill does it say that he must put the car back together. Is this a freebee which is being handed to the minister? Does he hand back the car after he is finished with it? How does it work? When I read that section of the proposed act, 1 chuckled to myself because 1 could see the minister tearing apart an automobile behind the Parliament buildings to see what makes it tick. I would be surprised if he knew where to put the gas in his car because he never has to do it himself.
In concluding my brief remarks on the bill, I should like to talk about the reality of the situation. The reality is that the minister is not doing anything and that the made-in-Canada energy policy about which the minister talks so proudly is not being changed or improved one iota by the bill. If we look at the campaign promises of 1974 and at the Speech from the Throne in 1976, we realize that the government is making it appear as if it were doing something as part of its national energy policy but is really not changing anything. The goals supplied by Transport Canada to be reached by the auto industry are really meaningless. In fairness to Transport Canada, their rationale is that they must compare their data with the American tests. Only that fact makes sense.
When this bill goes to committee, I invite the minister to explain how he will have a different set of criteria when the automobile market is a North American market. There are many other ways in which the minister could likely achieve fuel efficiency. For instance, the reduction in the speed limit in the United States has had a great effect on fuel consumption there. There are still some provinces-I know speed limitation comes under provincial jurisdiction, I have been around a while, and I am glad the minister is listening-that allow a 70 mile per hour speed limit. I know that the minister does not get along that well with the provinces but perhaps he could use his bubbly personality and smiling countenance to persuade these provinces to cut back their speed limits.
Finally, the bill does not seem to accomplish what the government has indicated it will. 1 believe that once discussions have taken place in committee and once the Canadian people have seen this bill-the automobile manufacturers do not even know the bill exists-they will see that nothing has changed. Why are we wasting the time of the House with this bill? It is a public relations endeavour by the Minister of Energy, Mines
Fuel Consumption Standards
and Resources which in fact will not prove to be an integral part of the energy legislation and should not be lumped in with the National Energy Program because it is such a phony.
